topic: Google's Open Agentic Orchestrator (AX / Agent Executor): what it means for agent orchestration

key_points: Official Google Cloud announcement (May 20, 2026) by Jaana Dogan (SWE) and Ethan Bao (Eng Director); positions AX as an open-source runtime standard for agent execution, resumption and distributed deployment.

Five native capabilities claimed: durable execution (resume after outages/HITL), secure isolation (sandboxes), session consistency (single-writer), connection recovery (client reconnect backfills from last sequence seen), trajectory branching from checkpoints.

Federation story: bridges Google Antigravity, Google-built frontier agents (e.g. Deep Research), custom agents managed by Google (Managed Agents API), custom agents built with LangChain/LangGraph/ADK, and A2A-protocol agents.
Sovereignty pitch: prevent vendor lock-in, own your data plane (MCPs, skills, agents), harness-agnostic, choose your own compute and isolation boundaries.

Scale claim: partnered with the GKE team on Agent Substrate because agents are nonlinear programs that wait for external input; Substrate moves agents on/off ready compute in real time and is designed for 'the chatter of millions of sub-second tool calls' plus hundreds of millions of registered agents.

Project landing page; states AX is 'a distributed agent runtime designed for reliability, safety, customizability, and efficiency' and that it is an open source project from Google (github.com/google/ax).

Six marketed properties: resumable/autonomous, customizable (tools, skills, purpose-built agents), Kubernetes-native on Agent Substrate, model- and harness-agnostic, protocol support (MCP, A2A), auditing/policies with full audit trail and trajectory collection.
Install path is a single Go command: go install github.com/google/ax/cmd/ax@latest.
Repo self-describes as 'Google's open agentic orchestration runtime' and as Agent Executor (AX): a distributed harness runtime that provisions isolated environments from suspendable/resumable images.

Features: distributed runtime, resumption, built-in harnesses, portability, customizability (custom env, MCP tools, skills, instructions). Consistency features: single-writer architecture, event log, advanced compute-layer actor resumption.

Docs/CLI are deliberately kubectl-shaped: ax apply / get / describe / watch / delete / ssh, plus agent-specific verbs; tasks are immutable once created; suspend/resume are first-class RPCs (SuspendTask, ResumeTask, WatchTask streaming).

Architecture (DESIGN.md): state lives in Redis, not etcd — storing millions of short-lived tasks as Kubernetes CRDs would exceed etcd comfort limits; binaries are ax (CLI), ax-server (gRPC on :8080, /healthz), ax-task-runner (PID 1 inside every task container).

Roadmap: stabilize ax.io/v1alpha1 specs (Task/Workspace/Model/Sandbox), new Agent Substrate Actor migration, separate workspace-setup actor, least-privilege setup vs runtime policies, idleness detection + automatic suspension for density, stateful task branching, SPIFFE identities for tasks, governance and telemetry.
Frames AX as a Kubernetes-style declarative orchestrator plus runtime (Apache 2.0) that treats agents as stateful actors rather than microservices or batch jobs.

Four core declarative primitives under the ax.io/v1alpha1 API group: Task (execution lifecycle, sandbox resource constraints), Workspace (pre-execution environment assembly: git repos, MCP servers, skill bundles, natural-language goal executed by an init agent), Gateway (outbound network allowlists/egress policy), Model (provider + parameters).

Explains the operational divergence: agents are stateful, bursty, long-running, spending most wall-clock idle while awaiting model tokens, tools, or HITL; naive Kubernetes keeps sandboxes hot during idle or pays cold-start latency on resume.
Sub-second suspension/resumption with zero cold start; dozens of tasks multiplexed onto shared host workers; architecture rooted in systems research across Google and Google DeepMind.

Forkast syndicated analysis: AX hit #1 on Hacker News on Sept 21, 2026 with 664 points and 299 comments; the paradox is a familiar kubectl-shaped interface bolted to a heavy Kubernetes dependency that splits the community.

Distinguishes interface from engine: AX is the declarative layer; Agent Substrate is the compute runtime using gVisor isolation and GCS-backed pod snapshots for sub-second suspend/resume, described as 'Actor Teleport'.

Quotes co-creator Jaana Dogan on HN: 'AX is a layer that is closer to job orchestration... It's NOT an agentic framework.' Substrate bypasses the standard Kubernetes control plane on the hot path to target hundreds of millions of registered agents.
Notable timing puzzle: the project was announced May 20, 2026 but only surged on HN in late September 2026 — late discovery or a maturity threshold, not a new launch.
666-point front-page thread on 'AX – Google's Open Agentic Orchestrator' — the primary source of skeptical practitioner consensus used across secondary coverage.

Co-creator rakyll answers the framing criticism: they do mention Agent Substrate, and Substrate 'is working on Kubernetes but isn't exclusive to Kubernetes'; AX targets teams that want one stack on any cluster and who struggle to deliver agentic apps onto someone else's compute.

Practitioner objection (jauntywundrkind): with AX/Substrate you opt into a huge stack and must build for Substrate, unlike Scion which runs existing harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) locally and in-cluster.

Kubernetes ergonomics complaint is repeated verbatim by many: the README quickstart requires a cluster, ko, a pullable registry, and a reachable Agent Substrate control API — under a marketing line promising uncompromising ergonomics.

Identity/security answers from maintainers: Substrate is becoming an OIDC and SPIFFE IDP; an egress gateway injects credentials so agent containers never hold long-lived secrets; Google Agent Identity is already built around SPIFFE.

Ecosystem context in-thread: Substrate is moving to CNCF (cncf/sandbox#523), kagent has experimental Substrate support, and agent-sandbox (sigs.k8s.io) is the k8s-native cousin with a different tradeoff.

Google-track-record skepticism dominates the top comments (killedbygoogle.com, 'k8sification of AI', 'LOL. Bye!' at the cluster requirement) — a real objection the article must answer rather than dismiss.

Hands-on setup walkthrough: Go toolchain, a Kubernetes cluster, ko, a registry nodes can pull, and a reachable Substrate control API (in-cluster default api.ate-system.svc.cluster.local:443); then make deploy AX_IMAGE_REPO=<your-registry> lands Redis + control plane in the ax-system namespace.

Operational loop: ax apply -f task.yaml, then wait on the WorkspaceReady and Ready conditions rather than the phase string; keep debug: true while learning because guest services (and therefore ax ssh) stay off without it.
Confidence test before a multi-hour job: ax ssh in, write a file, ax suspend task, ax resume task, ssh back and confirm the file survived.

Honest limitations section: egress hostname allowlists can block all TLS egress (start with host '*' on 443 and tighten); Task env values are plain, with no valueFrom and no clean secret mount story (issue #348 territory); WorkspaceReady can flip true on empty git clones (issue #347) so always verify over ax ssh.
Positions AX under LangGraph/ADK/CrewAI rather than against them: run LangGraph as the Task command; the pitch is that the sandbox layer and its state survive when the Python process does not.

Sharpest conceptual distinction available: both AX and modern harnesses center on an append-only event log, but they record different things — a harness logs what the model saw (prompts, reasoning, tool calls, context injections) while AX logs what the task did (process state, filesystem, scheduling).

'One log lets you ask why the model chose something. The other lets you kill the machine and continue. Neither substitutes for the other.' — the correct mental model for where a runtime stops and a framework begins.

Notes the primitives are deliberately none of them prompts: Task (isolated execution with CPU/memory limits), Workspace (git repos, MCP servers, skills), Gateway (network policy), Model (provider config) — no planner, no graph, no agent loop.
Observation worth reusing: AX's four primitives are workload-shaped, not prompt-shaped, which is why it can host harnesses from any vendor and why it does not compete with them.

Side-by-side framing of Google's two late-2026 open-source agent projects: Scion for coordinating teams of agents (one isolated container + optional git worktree per agent, coordination via CLI so the model decides when to collaborate) and AX for resumable single-agent infrastructure.

Explains the concrete failure Scion prevents: three Claude Code agents editing one repository read the same file and overwrite each other; container isolation separates processes while worktree isolation separates files.
Both are Apache 2.0 Go projects created in March 2026 — evidence that Google is shipping agent infrastructure in layers (coordination, execution) rather than one monolithic framework.
Agent Substrate's CNCF Sandbox application (filed Sept 8, 2026) — the strongest available signal that the layer under AX is being made vendor-neutral rather than kept as a Google Cloud moat.

Roadmap context: target sub-100ms p95 activation latency through tiered snapshot caching (local zswap, local SSD, peer-to-peer, object storage), incremental snapshots, and disk-only resume modes for cold-start agents.

Declares Kubernetes reliance for provisioning, WorkerPool pod lifecycle, CRD reconciliation (atecontroller) and node scheduling, plus Envoy for the atenet-router ingress gateway; CRDs include WorkerPool, ActorTemplate, SandboxConfig.

Governance disclosure states Google's business model is 'strictly infrastructure-centric' — users run the open-source stack on VMs they buy and manage; maintainer diversity (16 of 18 from one org) flagged as a non-blocking TOC item.

stats.fact: google/ax has 12,550 stars, 612 forks, 59 open issues, is Apache-2.0 licensed, written in Go, created 2026-03-30 and last pushed 2026-09-27 per the GitHub API (a GitHub page snapshot in the same day showed ~1,955 stars, so quote API-scale numbers, not a stale page render).

Release cadence is early and fast: v0.3.1 (2026-09-25), v0.3.0 (2026-09-20), v0.2.3 (2026-08-13), v0.2.2 (2026-07-23), v0.2.1 and v0.2.0 (2026-07-22), v0.1.0 — still pre-1.0 with breaking changes explicitly expected.

AX reached #1 on Hacker News on 2026-09-21 with 664 points and 299 comments; secondary snapshots of the same thread report 621/284 and 179/74, so cite a point-in-time figure with the date attached rather than a single 'final' number.

AX was announced May 20, 2026 by Jaana Dogan and Ethan Bao on the Google Cloud blog, but the Hacker News surge did not happen until September 21, 2026 — roughly four months later, which is why many late-September write-ups misdate the launch.

Agent Substrate claims sub-500ms resume, 500+ suspend/resume activations per second, and 10x higher sandbox density than standard container runtimes; its demo multiplexes ~250 stateful actors across 8 physical pods (30x+ oversubscription).

Agent Substrate has 3,962 stars and 473 forks, created 2026-05-13, last pushed 2026-09-29 — it lives in a non-Google GitHub org (agent-substrate/) and is in the process of being donated to the CNCF as vendor-neutral common ground.

Substrate's roadmap targets sub-100ms p95 actor activation latency via tiered snapshot caching (local zswap, local SSD, peer-to-peer, object storage) plus disk-only resume modes — i.e. today's sub-second is a waypoint, not the ceiling.

The resume path is a real distributed transaction: CoreDNS → Envoy (ext_proc) → ateapi workflow engine under a 30s lock → Redis state → atelet on the hosting node → 'runsc restore' into a gVisor sandbox, then a header rewrite to route to the pod IP.
The four AX primitives are Task, Workspace, Gateway and Model in the ax.io/v1alpha1 API group — there is no planner, graph, memory or prompt abstraction anywhere in the surface.

Comparison anchors for 2026: kagent 3,885 stars (CNCF Sandbox, agents as CRDs, built by Istio founders, experimental Agent Substrate support), Scion 1,729 stars (GoogleCloudPlatform org, multi-agent coordination with one container + optional git worktree per agent, carries a 'not an officially supported Google product' disclaimer).

AX's state does not live in etcd: DESIGN.md states that storing millions of short-lived tasks as Kubernetes CRDs would exceed etcd's single-digit-GB and write-rate comfort zone, so AX persists to Redis and reconciles directly with Agent Substrate under distributed locks.

Known alpha-state defects documented by practitioners in late September 2026: WorkspaceReady can report ready on an empty git clone (#347), Task env has no valueFrom/secret-mount story (#348 territory), hostname-style egress allowlists can block all TLS egress, and a security report (#337) covers per-request harness_config overlay allowing process spawn via mcp_servers.

Governance identity roadmap is SPIFFE-based: tasks are to receive SPIFFE IDs / X.509-SVIDs for zero-trust mTLS, and the Substrate egress gateway injects actor credentials into outbound requests so sandboxes never hold long-lived secrets.

Google's own framing of the scale target is hundreds of millions of registered agents and billions of tasks per cluster, with Agent Substrate bypassing the standard Kubernetes control plane on the hot path for the 'chatter of millions of sub-second tool calls'.

Caution flag: a widely surfaced aggregator post (dev.to, later 404) attributes AX to a September 18 I/O unveil with a modular DAG engine, a Gemini 1.5 Pro reference implementation and a 27% benchmark win over LangChain — none of which appear in the repo, docs, or Google's blog. Treat such specifics as fabricated.

angles: Category correction first: AX is not another agent framework. Co-creator Jaana Dogan's own words — 'AX is a layer that is closer to job orchestration... It's NOT an agentic framework' — make the article's spine: orchestrator/runtime (AX + Substrate) sits underneath the framework (ADK, LangGraph) and harness (Antigravity, Claude Code) you already use, and you can run LangGraph as the Task command.

The idle-time economics nobody prices: an agent's wall-clock life is mostly waiting on model tokens, tool round-trips, or human approval; naive Kubernetes charges full compute for that waiting or pays cold-start latency on resume. Sub-second suspend/resume plus 30x oversubscription is the actual product, and it reframes orchestration from a control-flow problem into a capacity problem.

Layered-bill of materials: Google shipped the coordination layer (Scion), the execution runtime (Agent Substrate, headed to CNCF) and the declarative control plane (AX) in one year. Explain which layer you actually need — most teams need one, not three.

Event-log semantics as the conceptual payoff: 'a harness logs what the model saw; AX logs what the task did.' One lets you audit reasoning, the other lets you kill the machine and continue. Conflating checkpointing with model memory is the most common review mistake in this space.

The Kubernetes objection answered honestly: the ergonomics marketing line and the cluster+ko+registry+Substrate Control API quickstart sit in the same README. Cover who is genuinely served (platform teams already running GKE) and who is not (a developer with a laptop and one agent).

Alpha-state receipts: cite the concrete open issues (#347 empty-clone WorkspaceReady, #348 secret handling, #337 security overlay, egress allowlist footgun) and the README's own PR freeze plus 'major breaking changes prior to a stable release' warning. This is the differentiator versus tutorial-style posts that only repeat the pitch.

Vendor-neutrality test: AX itself sits in the google org with no support disclaimer, while the layer it depends on is being donated to CNCF (cncf/sandbox#523) with a stated 16-of-18-single-org maintainer caveat. Explain what CNCF ownership does and does not buy an adopter.

Migration-cost framing: switching cost is not the CLI, it is rebuilding workloads for Substrate actors (Kubernetes Jobs do not run in a secure runtime; no CRDs on the hot path; routing via ate-target-actor header rather than per-task Services).

Practical decision matrix: AX vs kagent (agents as CRDs, k8s-native, GitOps) vs Scion (run existing harnesses, multi-agent coordination) vs Temporal/LangGraph durable execution (workflow-level durability without a sandbox runtime).

Governance roadmap as a hedge: SPIFFE task identity, egress gateway credential injection, budget guardrails, telemetry/trajectory collection — the enterprise checklist that determines whether AX is adoptable in regulated environments, currently mostly roadmap rather than shipped.
